cards.title: Relatedly: Scaffolding Literature Reviews with Existing Related Work Sections
cards.meta: CHI 2023 · doi 10.1145/3544548.3580841 · comparison only, zero credit

rows.value: The problem is built citation by citation and each step holds. Publication counts are rising and fields are mixing; survey papers answer this where they exist and go stale where they do not; search engines find papers but leave the connections between them to the reader, which is cited as the step nobody supports; and the graph and cluster tools that try to show those connections are faulted with a specific finding, that automatic clusters conflate several dimensions at once and readers cannot work out what a cluster means. Against that sits the observation the whole system rests on, cited to two sources, that authors already summarise and connect prior work in their related work sections, and that each such paragraph carries context and structure around the papers it names. Information foraging theory supplies the interaction: people alternate between exploring new patches and exploiting one they have found, and read scent cues to judge whether a source is worth the time, so the interface shows how much unread material each paragraph would bring and lets a reader drop into similar paragraphs. The discussion adds a finding from educational psychology, that several explanations of the same topic help people make sense of it, offered afterwards as the reason the approach worked.

Every paper contains a small, current review of its own corner of a field, written by somebody who read the work. This system collects those related work paragraphs from many papers and searches them by topic rather than by paper, so a reader sees several authors framing the same area in different ways. It ranks paragraphs so the first ones cover the widest spread of subtopics, writes a heading for any paragraph whose own heading says nothing, greys out references the reader has already met and highlights the ones they have not, and shows how much of the space is still unread. Fifteen researchers spent twenty minutes building an outline for a survey on each of two topics, once with this and once with a paper search engine. This card does not refilter the paper.

rows.value: 1 INTRODUCTION: surveys that are unavailable or out of date, search engines that find papers but not themes, and the proposal to read many papers' related work sections on one topic instead (PDF pp. 1–3); 2 RELATED WORK: what a literature review is for and why doing one from individual papers overloads the reader, information foraging as the account of how people explore, and the cluster tools whose groupings cannot be read (PDF pp. 3–4)

read to prove design operationalization · 3 AND 4, FORMATIVE STUDY AND SYSTEM: ten scholars interviewed over a plain search engine on the same corpus, then a system that ranks paragraphs for coverage, generates missing headings, and marks references as seen or unseen (PDF pp. 4–9); 5 STUDY DESIGN: fifteen researchers, two topics and two systems counterbalanced, twenty minutes each, the baseline given the same papers and one-click access to the same paragraphs, outlines written in a shared document (PDF pp. 9–11); 6 FINDINGS: outlines rated blind by two topic experts for coherence, insight and detail, behaviour logs counting paragraphs and papers touched, a preference question, a workload scale, and five people who kept using it (PDF pp. 11–14); 7 DISCUSSION: multiple explanations of one topic offered as the mechanism, foraging offered as the account of the logs, and limitations covering the corpus, the single baseline and the junior sample (PDF pp. 14–17)

The word scaffolding is in the title and the support is never withdrawn. Everything measured here is measured with the tool open: the outline is written during the twenty minutes, the log counts what was touched during those twenty minutes, and the preference is asked immediately afterwards. The outline is a record of the session, not of the reader, so a better outline means the session went better and not that the person now knows more, and the study makes no claim otherwise. The comparison is honest in a way worth noting, since the baseline was given the same corpus and a button that opens the same related work paragraphs, so the difference measured is the interface rather than the material. Two details are worth carrying forward. The first is a design decision that assumes exactly what nobody measures: the topics were varied across conditions to prevent carry-over effects in learning, which asserts that what a person picks up in one session persists into the next, and the design then arranges for that never to be tested. The second is the closest thing in this round to an unforced follow-up. Five participants asked to keep the system afterwards for real reviews of their own, used it unpaid and unobliged for between one and a half and twenty-five hours over two weeks, and were interviewed about it. One of them describes a learning curve in getting used to reading paragraphs rather than papers, and says it becomes easier once you are used to the paradigm. That is a claim about learning the tool rather than the topic, but it is at least a claim made after the novelty wore off, which is more than a lab session can give.
